_note: Batch 1a — drums and low end. 36 answers against canonical ids from v2/QUESTION_BANK.md. Every number here is a starting point for a real source, not a preset: the steps say what to listen for so the user can move off the number.

questions.q: How do I tighten up my kick?
questions.short: Shorten the tail, do not shrink the hit. Gate the decay and cut the long low resonance.
steps: Gate or fade the kick so the tail ends before the next transient, around 120–200 ms.
Find the ringing note by sweeping a narrow boost between 80 and 200 Hz, then cut it 3–5 dB.
High-pass at 30–40 Hz to remove rumble that reads as looseness, not weight.
Check against the bass: often the flab is the bass, not the kick.
questions.why: A loose kick is almost always a long low-frequency decay rather than a soft attack. Shortening the tail leaves the transient untouched, so the kick gets tighter without getting smaller.
questions.watch: Gate too hard and the kick loses its body entirely. Set the gate to reduce by 10–15 dB, not to silence.

questions.q: How do I make my kick sound bigger?
questions.short: Size is low-end sustain plus harmonics that let small speakers imply the fundamental.
steps: Lift 2–3 dB at 50–70 Hz with a wide bell, not a shelf.
Add saturation after the EQ so the 100–200 Hz harmonics carry the weight on phones.
Lengthen the decay slightly or layer a longer sub sample underneath, tuned to the key.
Clear 200–400 Hz on everything else before you add more to the kick.
questions.why: Phone and laptop speakers cannot reproduce 60 Hz at all. The harmonics saturation adds let the ear infer the fundamental that is not physically there, which is why a saturated kick sounds bigger everywhere, not just on monitors.
questions.watch: Bigger low end eats headroom fast. Watch the master meter while you do this, not after.

questions.q: Why does my kick sound boxy?
questions.short: Too much 250–500 Hz, usually from a close mic inside the shell or an untreated room.
steps: Sweep a narrow boost from 250 to 500 Hz, find the worst spot, cut it 3–6 dB.
Use a moderately narrow Q, around 2–3. Wider than that and you lose the body with it.
If it is still boxy after the cut, the problem is the room, not the kick.
Re-check in context — a little box in solo is often inaudible in the mix.
questions.why: That band is where a drum shell's own resonance lives. Close-miking inside the drum exaggerates it, and small untreated rooms add their own peak in the same place.
questions.watch: Cut too much and the kick goes thin and papery. The fix is usually 3–4 dB, not 10.

questions.q: Why does my kick sound muddy?
questions.short: The kick is probably fine. Mud at 150–300 Hz is usually the bass and the kick summing.
steps: Solo the kick. If it is clean alone, the problem is the overlap, not the kick.
Cut 2–3 dB at 150–250 Hz on whichever of the two is less important to the song.
High-pass everything that is not kick or bass at 80–120 Hz first.
Only then touch the kick itself.
questions.why: Two sources each contributing 2 dB at 200 Hz sum to roughly 4 dB there. Neither sounds wrong in solo, which is exactly why soloing to find mud almost never works.
questions.watch: If cutting the kick makes the mix thin, you cut the wrong source. Put it back and cut the bass instead.

questions.q: Why does my kick sound thin?
questions.short: You high-passed it too high, or you are hearing a sample with no sustain at all.
steps: Move the high-pass down to 30 Hz or turn it off and listen again.
Check the sample: many free kicks are all click and no body. Layer a sub under it.
Lift 2 dB at 60–80 Hz, wide, before you reach for anything else.
Confirm on headphones — small monitors lie about this constantly.
questions.why: Advice to high-pass everything comes from mixing live multitrack, where every mic has rumble. On a clean sample there is nothing below the fundamental to remove, so the filter only removes the kick.
questions.watch: If adding low end makes the mix worse rather than the kick better, the headroom is the problem.

questions.q: How do I make my kick brighter?
questions.short: Lift the beater around 3–5 kHz, or layer a click. Brightness here is attack, not air.
steps: Boost 2–3 dB at 3–5 kHz with a medium Q. That is the beater, not the shell.
If the sample has nothing up there to lift, layer a short click sample instead.
Use a transient designer to raise attack rather than EQ if the body is already right.
Check on a phone speaker — this band is exactly what small speakers reproduce.
questions.why: A kick above 8 kHz is just noise; there is no useful content there. Everything the ear reads as definition in a kick sits between 2 and 6 kHz, which is also the band a phone speaker handles best.
questions.watch: Too much and the kick starts clicking like a metronome, especially in dense arrangements.

questions.q: How do I tighten up my snare?
questions.short: Find the ring note and notch it, then shorten the sustain rather than compressing harder.
steps: Sweep a narrow boost from 300 Hz to 1 kHz to find the ring, then cut it 4–6 dB with a Q of 4–6.
Use a transient designer and pull sustain down 2–4 rather than adding compression.
Tighten the gate release before you touch the threshold.
Leave the top end alone — ring is a mid problem.
questions.why: Snare ring is a single resonant note, so a narrow cut removes it without touching the crack above it or the body below. Compression would duck the whole drum to control one frequency.
questions.watch: A notch that narrow can make the snare sound processed in solo and perfect in the mix. Judge it in context.

questions.q: How do I make my snare sound bigger?
questions.short: Room and parallel compression make a snare big. EQ alone just makes it louder.
steps: Send the snare to a short room reverb, 0.6–1.2 s, with 10–20 ms pre-delay.
Parallel-compress a copy at 8:1 or 10:1, smashed, and blend it underneath.
Add 1–2 dB at 180–240 Hz for body before you touch the top end.
High-pass the reverb return at 300 Hz so the size does not add mud.
questions.why: Size is a time-domain cue, not a frequency one. The ear reads the length of the decay and the density of reflections as how big the room was, which EQ cannot imitate.
questions.watch: Long room tails smear fast tempos. Shorten the decay before you lower the send.

questions.q: Why does my snare sound boxy?
questions.short: Too much 400–800 Hz. Cut it narrow, and check the overheads are not carrying it too.
steps: Sweep 400–800 Hz with a narrow boost, find the worst spot, cut 3–5 dB.
Check the overheads and room mics — they usually have the same peak.
If the kit sounds boxy as a whole, cut it once on the drum bus instead of five times.
Confirm with the bass muted; low-mid buildup can read as box.
questions.why: The shell's fundamental resonance sits in this band and every microphone pointed at the kit picks it up, so the same peak gets added three or four times across the kit.
questions.watch: Cutting it on every channel separately hollows out the kit. Pick one place and do it there.

questions.q: Why does my snare sound harsh?
questions.short: A narrow peak between 2 and 4 kHz, often created by the compressor rather than the drum.
steps: Bypass the compressor. If the harshness goes, slow the attack to 10–15 ms.
If it stays, sweep 2–4 kHz with a narrow boost and cut the peak 3–5 dB.
Try a dynamic EQ on that band so it only cuts on the loudest hits.
Saturate gently afterwards — it rounds the edge without dulling the crack.
questions.why: A fast compressor attack clamps the body of the hit and leaves the transient peak standing proud, which the ear reads as harshness. Slowing the attack lowers the peak relative to everything around it.
questions.watch: Cutting 2–4 kHz too hard loses the snare entirely in a dense mix. Small moves, checked in context.

questions.q: Why does my snare sound thin?
questions.short: The body at 150–250 Hz has been filtered out, or you are only hearing the top mic.
steps: Lower the high-pass to 80–100 Hz and listen again.
Lift 2–3 dB at 180–220 Hz with a wide bell for body.
Bring up the bottom snare mic if you have one, and check its polarity.
Add parallel compression rather than more EQ if it is still thin.
questions.why: A snare's body and its crack live two octaves apart. Filtering aggressively to clean the low mids removes the body and leaves only the crack, which reads as thin however loud it gets.
questions.watch: If the bottom mic makes it thinner rather than fuller, flip its polarity before adjusting anything else.

questions.q: How do I make my snare wider?
questions.short: Widen the room and the overheads, never the snare itself. The snare stays centred.
steps: Leave the close mic dead centre and mono.
Send it to a stereo room reverb and widen that return instead.
Bring up the overheads, which already carry stereo information.
Check mono: if the snare drops in level, something is out of phase.
questions.why: The snare is a timekeeper and the ear expects it in the centre with the kick. Widening the source itself makes the groove feel unanchored; widening its reflections gives size without moving it.
questions.watch: Stereo wideners on a snare are the fastest way to destroy mono compatibility.

questions.q: How do I make my hats brighter?
questions.short: Use a shelf above 10 kHz, not a bell at 5 kHz. The second one just makes them harsh.
steps: High-pass the hats at 300–500 Hz first; you will hear brightness without boosting anything.
Add a gentle shelf of 1.5–3 dB above 10 kHz.
If they are still dull, the sample is dull — swap it rather than boosting 6 dB.
Keep 4–7 kHz flat. That band is where harshness lives, not air.
questions.why: Removing low mids raises the perceived brightness of everything above them, so the filter does half the job for free and costs no headroom.
questions.watch: Bright hats become fatiguing over a three-minute song in a way they do not over a four-bar loop.

questions.q: Why do my hats sound like white noise?
questions.short: A peak at 6–9 kHz, and usually too many layered hat samples stacking in the same band.
steps: Count your hat layers. Three samples in the same band is the usual cause.
Cut 3–4 dB at 6–9 kHz with a medium Q on the busiest layer.
Use a de-esser on the hat bus set to 7 kHz instead of a static cut.
Lower the velocity of the repeated hits rather than compressing the whole part.
questions.why: Hat noise is broadband, so layers add energy across the whole top end instead of at one frequency. The result climbs faster than any single layer suggests it should.
questions.watch: Over-cutting here makes the whole mix sound covered, because the same band carries vocal consonants.

questions.q: How do I smooth out my hats?
questions.short: Edit the velocities before you compress. A compressor cannot fix a programming problem.
steps: Lower the velocity on the off-beat hits by 15–25 so the pattern breathes.
Then compress lightly, 2:1 with 1–2 dB of gain reduction, to level what is left.
Add a touch of saturation instead of more compression if it still feels spiky.
For rolls, automate the level down across the roll rather than compressing it.
questions.why: Programmed hats at a single velocity have no dynamic shape, so a compressor has nothing to level and just adds pumping. Varying velocity creates the groove the compressor is supposed to flatter.
questions.watch: Heavy compression on hats pulls up the noise floor between hits, which sounds like hiss.

questions.q: How do I push my hats further back?
aliases: hats are too loud in the mix
questions.short: Roll off the top rather than pulling the fader; level alone keeps them feeling close.
steps: Add a low-pass or high shelf, cutting 2–4 dB above 10 kHz.
Pan them 15–30% off centre so they stop competing with the vocal's centre.
Add a short reverb send, 0.4–0.8 s, to place them behind the snare.
Then lower the fader, last, by 1–2 dB.
questions.why: Distance in the real world removes high frequencies before it removes level. Darkening a source makes the ear place it further away even when its volume has not changed.
questions.watch: Too dark and the hats stop defining the groove. Keep enough top to hear the pattern.

questions.q: Why do my toms sound boomy?
aliases: too much low end on toms
questions.short: Each tom has one resonant note. Find it, cut it narrow, and gate the rest.
steps: Sweep each tom separately between 80 and 300 Hz to find its own ring, and cut 4–6 dB.
Gate the toms so they are silent when nobody is hitting them.
High-pass the floor tom at 50 Hz and the rack toms at 80–100 Hz.
Check the overheads — tom boom often arrives through them, not the close mics.
questions.why: Toms resonate sympathetically whenever the kick or snare is struck, so their mics are open and ringing for the whole song even though the toms are played in four bars of it.
questions.watch: Gates that are too aggressive cut the start of the tom fill. Set the gate with the fill, not the verse.

questions.q: How do I make my toms hit harder?
questions.short: Slow attack to keep the stick, then add body at 100–200 Hz and attack at 4–6 kHz.
steps: Compress at 4:1, attack 20–30 ms, release 150–250 ms, 4–6 dB of gain reduction.
Lift 2–3 dB at 100–200 Hz for the floor tom, higher for the racks.
Add 2 dB at 4–6 kHz for the stick on the head.
Parallel-compress the tom bus and blend it in under the dry toms.
questions.why: Toms have a long decay relative to their attack, so a fast compressor flattens the hit and leaves the boom. A slow attack lets the stick through and compresses only the sustain.
questions.watch: Long releases on toms pump the bleed from the rest of the kit. Gate first, compress second.

questions.q: Why do my toms disappear in the mix?
aliases: toms sound fine soloed but not in the mix
questions.short: They are competing with the bass below and the guitars above. Carve, do not push.
steps: Duck the bass 2–3 dB during tom fills with a sidechain or an automation ride.
Cut 2 dB at 400–600 Hz on the guitars or keys where the toms need to sit.
Lift the stick at 4–6 kHz rather than raising the whole tom.
Automate the tom fader up 2–3 dB for the fills only.
questions.why: Toms appear for two bars in a four-minute song, so a static balance that works for the verse will always bury them. This is an automation problem wearing an EQ problem's clothes.
questions.watch: Raising toms globally makes the bleed in their mics louder for the whole song.

questions.q: How do I make my overheads wider?
questions.short: Widen with mid/side on the sides only, and check mono before you commit to any of it.
steps: Raise the side signal 2–3 dB with a mid/side plugin rather than using a widener.
High-pass the side channel at 300 Hz so the low end stays centred.
Pan the close mics to match what the overheads show, not the other way round.
Fold to mono: if the cymbals drop noticeably, reduce the side boost.
questions.why: Mid/side widening raises what is already different between the channels instead of generating fake difference with delay, so it survives a mono fold where a Haas-based widener does not.
questions.watch: If the close mics and the overheads disagree about where the snare is, the kit sounds confused however wide it is.

questions.q: Why do my overheads sound harsh?
questions.short: Cut 3–6 kHz, not 10 kHz. Harsh cymbals are a mid problem that sounds like a top problem.
steps: Sweep 3–6 kHz with a narrow boost, find the worst spot, cut 3–4 dB.
High-pass at 300–400 Hz to remove the shell boom the overheads also capture.
Use a de-esser on the overhead bus tuned to 5 kHz for only the loudest crashes.
Leave the air above 12 kHz alone — that is where the cymbals sound expensive.
questions.why: The ear is most sensitive around 3–4 kHz, so a cymbal peak there is perceived as pain while the same energy at 12 kHz is perceived as air.
questions.watch: Low-passing the overheads to fix harshness kills the cymbals and the kit's sense of a real room.

questions.q: Why do my overheads sound phasey?
questions.short: The two mics were not equidistant from the snare. Nudge one until mono stops thinning.
steps: Fold to mono and solo the overheads. Listen to the snare level as you work.
Nudge one overhead by a few samples until the snare is loudest in mono.
Check the close snare mic against the overheads the same way.
Flip the polarity of the bottom snare mic if you have one.
questions.why: If one mic is further from the snare than the other, the same hit arrives at two different times and partially cancels when summed. Aligning them is a timing fix, not an EQ one.
questions.watch: Aligning overheads to the snare can misalign them from the kick. Pick whichever matters more in the song.

questions.q: How do I make my drum bus hit harder?
questions.short: One compressor, slow attack, release timed to the tempo, 2–4 dB. Then parallel for the rest.
steps: Bus compressor at 4:1, attack 30 ms, release set so the needle returns by the next beat.
Aim for 2–4 dB of gain reduction, no more. This is glue, not the punch itself.
Run a parallel bus smashed at 10:1 and blend it under for the weight.
Saturate the parallel bus, not the main one.
questions.why: On a bus, a slow attack lets every transient through before gain reduction starts, so the kit gets denser between the hits while the hits themselves stay sharp.
questions.watch: Release too slow and the kit stops breathing between beats. Time it to the tempo, not by feel.

questions.q: Why is my drum bus pumping?
aliases: compression is pumping on my drums
questions.short: The release is longer than the gap between hits, so the compressor never recovers in time.
steps: Shorten the release until the gain reduction meter returns to zero before the next hit.
Lower the ratio to 2:1 or 3:1 before you raise the threshold.
High-pass the compressor's sidechain at 80–100 Hz so the kick stops triggering everything.
If you want some pump, keep it — just make sure it is in time with the tempo.
questions.why: Pumping is simply gain reduction that has not finished recovering when the next transient arrives, so each hit starts from a different gain. The sidechain filter fixes the most common cause: the kick dominating the detector.
questions.watch: Auto-release hides pumping rather than solving it, and takes the decision away from you.

questions.q: How do I make my drum bus louder without it falling apart?
aliases: drums clip when I push them
questions.short: Clip the peaks before the limiter. A few dB of soft clipping buys more than any fader.
steps: Soft-clip 2–4 dB off the loudest transients before anything else in the chain.
Then compress gently, 2:1 and 2–3 dB, to raise the body.
Cut 2–3 dB at 200–400 Hz; low-mid buildup is what limits drum loudness.
Only now raise the fader.
questions.why: Drum loudness is limited by the single loudest transient, which is usually a snare peak nobody can hear as a peak. Clipping it costs nothing audible and gives you back several decibels of average level.
questions.watch: Clipping sounds fine on drums and terrible on sustained sources. Keep it on this bus.

questions.q: How do I clean up my percussion?
questions.short: High-pass everything, pan the layers apart, and mute whichever two you notice least.
steps: High-pass every percussion part at 200–400 Hz. None of them need low end.
Pan them across the field so no two share a position.
Give each one a different band: shaker up top, conga in the low mids, bell in the presence range.
Mute each part in turn. Whichever you do not miss, leave muted.
questions.why: Percussion clutter is a spatial problem more often than a frequency one. Five parts stacked in the centre fight; the same five spread across the field read as one groove.
questions.watch: High-passing a conga or djembe too high removes the thump that makes it a drum.

questions.q: How do I make my percussion brighter?
questions.short: Shelf above 8 kHz and let transient shaping do the rest; shakers need attack, not treble.
steps: High-pass at 300 Hz first, then add a 2 dB shelf above 8 kHz.
Raise attack on a transient designer by 3–5 for shakers and tambourines.
Keep the brightest part the one carrying the groove, and leave the others darker.
Check on a phone — percussion is often the only thing audible up there.
questions.why: A shaker's perceived brightness comes mostly from the sharpness of its attack rather than its spectral balance, which is why transient shaping often works where EQ just adds hiss.
questions.watch: Brightening every percussion part at once produces a wash of noise. Pick one to lead.

questions.q: How do I make my 808 sound bigger?
questions.short: Saturate it. Size on real speakers comes from harmonics, not from more 40 Hz.
steps: Tune the 808 to the key of the song first. Nothing else matters as much.
Add saturation until the harmonics at 100–300 Hz are clearly audible on a laptop.
Lengthen the decay so it rings into the next beat, then gate it off before the kick.
Keep it mono below 120 Hz.
questions.why: Most listeners never hear the fundamental of an 808 at all. The ear reconstructs the missing pitch from its harmonics, so saturation is what makes it big on a phone and EQ at 40 Hz is what makes it big only in your room.
questions.watch: Over-saturated 808s turn into distorted bass guitars and stop feeling like sub.

questions.q: How do I tighten up my 808?
questions.short: Shorten the decay to the note length and sidechain it to the kick, 2–4 dB.
steps: Set the 808's decay so each note ends before the next one starts.
Sidechain to the kick, 2–4 dB, 10 ms attack, release before the next hit.
High-pass at 25–30 Hz to remove inaudible rumble eating headroom.
Add a limiter on the 808 alone to hold the peaks steady.
questions.why: 808 notes overlapping each other is the single most common cause of a loose low end, because two sub notes a semitone apart sum into a slow beating that reads as mush.
questions.watch: Too much ducking makes the 808 stutter on fast kick patterns. Shorten the release first.

questions.q: Why does my 808 sound muddy?
questions.short: The saturation added too much 150–300 Hz. Cut there, not in the sub.
steps: Cut 2–4 dB at 150–300 Hz, which is where saturation piles up harmonics.
Check nothing else is in that band — keys and guitars usually are.
Keep the sub below 60 Hz untouched; that is not where mud lives.
If it is still muddy, the 808 is out of tune with the track.
questions.why: Saturation generates harmonics upward from the fundamental, so an 808 at 50 Hz dumps energy at 100, 150 and 200 Hz — precisely where mud accumulates.
questions.watch: Cutting the sub to fix mud removes the only thing the 808 is there for.

questions.q: How do I stop my 808 notes jumping in level?
questions.short: It is the room and the sample, not your compressor. Fix the levels note by note first.
steps: Draw clip gain on the loud notes before any processing. Low notes always read louder.
Then compress at 4:1 with a slow attack and 3–5 dB of gain reduction.
Follow with a limiter to catch what is left.
Check on headphones: monitors in an untreated room will lie about which notes are loud.
questions.why: Low notes contain more energy than high ones at the same perceived loudness, and your room reinforces some notes and cancels others, so what you hear as uneven is partly real and partly the room.
questions.watch: Compressing hard enough to level unedited 808s will suck the attack out of every note.

questions.q: How do I tighten up my bass?
questions.short: Compress twice, gently, and high-pass. Two 3 dB stages beat one 6 dB stage.
steps: Compressor one: 3:1, slow attack 30 ms, 3 dB of gain reduction, to shape.
Compressor two: 4:1, fast attack 5 ms, 3 dB, to level.
High-pass at 30–40 Hz to remove rumble that reads as looseness.
Cut any single resonant note you find between 80 and 200 Hz.
questions.why: A single compressor doing 6 dB has to work hard enough to be audible. Two doing 3 dB each reach the same consistency while each one stays below the threshold where you notice it working.
questions.watch: Stacking two fast compressors kills the pick attack. Keep the first one slow.

questions.q: Why does my bass sound muddy?
questions.short: Cut 200–350 Hz and add 700 Hz–1.5 kHz. Definition lives higher than people expect.
steps: Cut 3–4 dB at 200–350 Hz with a medium Q.
Add 2 dB at 700 Hz–1.5 kHz for the note definition and the string.
Saturate so the bass line is audible on a phone with no low end at all.
Check against the kick — one of them has to give up 150–250 Hz.
questions.why: Bass notes are identified by their harmonics, not their fundamentals. Adding definition an octave or two above the note makes the line readable without adding any low end at all.
questions.watch: Pushing 700 Hz–1.5 kHz too far makes the bass honky and brings it forward of the vocal.

questions.q: Why does my bass disappear in the mix?
aliases: bass sounds fine soloed but not in the mix
questions.short: It has no mid-range. Nobody hears bass through a laptop — they hear its harmonics.
steps: Add 2–3 dB at 800 Hz–2 kHz, the band small speakers actually reproduce.
Parallel-distort a copy of the bass and blend it in, keeping the clean signal for the low end.
Make sure the kick and bass are not both occupying 60–120 Hz.
Listen on your phone before and after. That is the test that matters.
questions.why: A laptop speaker rolls off below 400 Hz. If all the bass energy is below that, the bass line is literally absent for most listeners, no matter how good it sounds on monitors.
questions.watch: Parallel distortion can make the bass wander forward of the vocal. Keep it under the clean signal.

questions.q: How do I clean up my bass?
questions.short: Mono below 120 Hz, high-pass the rumble, and remove the one note the room is adding.
steps: Make everything below 120 Hz mono.
High-pass at 30 Hz. Nothing musical lives below that in most arrangements.
Sweep 80–200 Hz for the one note that jumps out and cut it 3–4 dB.
Remove fret and finger noise with a de-esser at 2–4 kHz if it is a DI.
questions.why: Stereo information below about 120 Hz carries no directional cue the ear can use, but it does halve your headroom and cause cancellation on club systems that sum to mono.
questions.watch: Do not mono the whole bass if it has a stereo chorus you like above 200 Hz. Only the low band.

questions.q: How do I get my bass more upfront?
questions.short: Compress harder for consistency, then add 1–2 kHz. Fader moves will not do it.
steps: Compress to 5–8 dB of gain reduction. Bass is the most compressed instrument in most mixes.
Add 2 dB at 1–2 kHz for the string and the pick.
Keep it dry. Any reverb on bass pushes it backwards immediately.
Cut the same band on whatever is in front of it, usually the guitars.
questions.why: A source feels upfront when it is consistently present rather than when it is loud. Heavy compression removes the quiet moments where the ear would otherwise lose it.
questions.watch: Compressing bass this hard exposes every buzz and fret noise in the performance.
